title: Assessing advanced theory of mind in middle childhood: psychometric evaluation and responsiveness to training of a comprehensive AToM battery.
abstract: This study examined the psychometric properties and responsiveness to training of a comprehensive Advanced Theory of Mind (AToM) Battery in middle childhood. In Study 1, 168 eight- to nine-year-old children participated (M = 8.61 years, SD = 0.64; 88 girls, 79 boys, one preferred not to say). Children completed the AToM Battery, the Strange Stories task, and measures of language, inhibition, working memory, and nonverbal intelligence. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) largely supported the proposed three-factor structure. At the same time, the CFA indicated that several items, particularly within the Social Reasoning component, showed comparatively weak loadings. The AToM Battery showed moderate convergent validity with the Strange Stories task, r = .37, p < .001. Language ability significantly predicted overall AToM performance, R = .16, with effects primarily driven by the Social Reasoning component, R = .15. In Study 2, 126 children completed the battery at pretest, posttest, and follow-up after participating in either a conversation-based training or a control training. Linear mixed-effects models indicated general improvements over time across groups. Training-specific gains emerged most consistently for Recognition of Transgressions of Social Norms at posttest [t(247.20) = 3.45, p < .001] and follow-up [t(247.20) = 3.23, p = .001]. Stability correlations in the control group indicated moderate temporal stability over a three-month interval, r = .55, p < .001. Overall, the findings support the AToM Battery as a multidimensional and psychometrically useful measure of advanced social-cognitive reasoning, while highlighting the importance of considering language demands and subscale-specific responsiveness.
